title: WHAT IF THE GOOD THING YOU DID FOR GOD WAS REALLY FOR THE APPLAUSE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE GOOD THING YOU DID FOR GOD WAS REALLY FOR THE APPLAUSE?
What Jesus Really Meant When He Warned Against Practicing Righteousness to Be Seen—and Why His Words May Expose Something in Us We Never Wanted to Admit
There is a terrifying possibility hidden inside the Christian life.
You can do the right thing…
for the wrong reason.
You can give.
You can pray.
You can fast.
You can serve.
You can post Scripture.
You can defend biblical truth.
You can tell people about Jesus.
You can raise your hands during worship, volunteer at church, help someone who is suffering, give money to someone who desperately needs it, and say words that are completely true…
while somewhere underneath all of it, almost invisible even to you, your heart is whispering:
I hope somebody notices.
That is where Jesus takes us in Matthew 6.
Not merely into our behavior.
Into our motives.
Into that hidden room inside the human heart where nobody sees the difference between worship and performance.
Nobody…
except God.
And perhaps that is why the warning of Jesus is so uncomfortable.
Because He does not merely ask:
“What did you do?”
He confronts us with the far more frightening question:
“Who were you hoping would see you do it?”
Matthew records Jesus saying:
“Προσέχετε δὲ τὴν δικαιοσύνην ὑμῶν μὴ ποιεῖν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς…”
Prosechete de tēn dikaiosynēn hymōn mē poiein emprosthen tōn anthrōpōn pros to theathēnai autois…
A careful rendering is:
“Beware of practicing your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them…”
—Matthew 6:1
Slow down.
Because one small Greek expression changes how we understand this entire warning:
πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς
pros to theathēnai autois
“In order to be seen by them.”
Jesus was not issuing a blanket prohibition against anyone ever seeing you do something righteous.
That cannot be what He meant.
Only moments earlier in the same Sermon on the Mount, Jesus had told His disciples to let their light shine before others so that people would see their good works and glorify their Father in heaven.
So Matthew 5 does not say, “Make sure nobody sees.”
And Matthew 6 does not contradict Matthew 5.
The difference is devastatingly simple.
In Matthew 5, people see the works…
and glorify God.
In Matthew 6, people see the works…
and the performer wants them to glorify him.
Same visibility.
Different audience of the heart.
That is the issue.
You can perform a good deed publicly without performing it for publicity.
And you can perform a good deed secretly while still fantasizing about being praised for it.
Jesus goes deeper than location.
He goes after intention.
He is exposing the theater hidden inside the human heart.
And suddenly this two-thousand-year-old sermon feels painfully modern.
Because we live in an age where almost everything can become content.
The meal.
The workout.
The vacation.
The grief.
The generosity.
The prayer.
The Bible study.
The ministry.
Even compassion can become content.
Even repentance can become branding.
Even humility can become a performance of humility.
You can help someone and immediately feel the temptation to tell everyone that you helped.
You can read your Bible and wonder whether the open Bible would make a good photograph.
You can give generously and secretly hope your name is mentioned.
You can write something about Jesus and repeatedly check whether people reacted to it.
You can preach against pride while feeding your own.
You can even say, “All glory to God,” while quietly wondering how many people admired the person who said it.
That is how subtle this becomes.
The problem is not that someone saw.
The problem is that being seen became the reward you were seeking.
Jesus continues His warning by speaking about giving.
When you give to the needy, He says, do not announce it like the hypocrites who seek honor from others.
Then comes one of the most sobering statements in the passage:
“They have received their reward.”
Think about that.
Jesus does not say they received nothing.
They received exactly what they wanted.
Attention.
Recognition.
Admiration.
Applause.
And that was the tragedy.
They traded the pleasure of the Father for the praise of the crowd.
They received their reward…
and it was painfully small.
A compliment.
A reputation.
A reaction.
A few seconds of admiration from people who will eventually forget their name.
Imagine standing before eternity having exchanged something heavenly for something that disappeared before bedtime.
But before we turn this passage into a weapon against somebody else, Jesus forces us to bring it home.
Because it is incredibly easy to read Matthew 6 and immediately think of a religious hypocrite we know.
A preacher.
A church leader.
A Christian influencer.
Someone who posts every good deed.
Someone whose spirituality always seems to have a camera nearby.
But Jesus did not give this warning so that we could become experts at diagnosing everybody else's motives.
He gave it so that we would examine our own.
So forget everyone else for a moment.
What happens inside you when nobody notices?
When you serve and nobody thanks you?
When you give and nobody knows?
When you sacrifice and somebody else gets the credit?
When you pray and there is nobody nearby to hear how spiritual you sound?
When you obey God and it produces no likes, no recognition, no platform, no applause?
Does obedience still feel worthwhile?
That question can uncover things years of religious activity managed to hide.
Because sometimes we do not realize how addicted we have become to human approval until God allows us to obey Him without receiving any.
And silence from people can become spiritual surgery.
Suddenly you discover whether Jesus was really enough.
Jesus then turns toward prayer.
He describes people who love praying where others can see them.
Notice the problem again.
Prayer itself is good.
Public prayer itself is not inherently sinful. Jesus Himself prayed where others could hear Him.
The poison is the audience of the heart.
A prayer supposedly addressed to God can secretly become a speech performed for people.
The lips say, “Father…”
while the heart says, “Everybody, listen to me.”
That should shake every Christian who has ever prayed publicly.
Every pastor.
Every worship leader.
Every ministry worker.
Every content creator.
Every person who has ever typed a prayer beneath a photograph.
Including us.
Especially us.
Because religious performance is dangerous precisely because it can look almost identical to genuine devotion.
Two people can pray the same words.
One is worshiping.
The other is performing.
Two people can give the same amount.
One wants the hungry person helped.
The other wants the room impressed.
Two people can share the same Bible verse.
One desperately wants someone to encounter Christ.
The other desperately wants engagement.
But heaven can.
That is why Jesus repeatedly brings the Father into the conversation.
Your Father sees.
Your Father knows.
Your Father rewards.
This is not merely a sermon against hypocrisy.
It is an invitation into freedom.
You do not have to spend your life auditioning anymore.
You already have an audience.
The only Audience whose judgment ultimately matters.
Your Father sees the prayer nobody applauded.
He sees the money quietly given.
He sees the temptation resisted at 2:17 in the morning when nobody would ever have known.
He sees the apology.
He sees the forgiveness.
He sees the meal you bought.
He sees you closing the door and weeping before Him.
He sees the Christian who serves for twenty years without becoming famous.
He sees the mother praying over her sleeping children.
He sees the exhausted father opening Scripture before work.
He sees the teenager refusing what everyone else is doing because Christ matters more.
He sees the believer who could have announced the sacrifice but chose silence.
He sees.
And when the approval of God becomes enough, the addiction to human applause begins losing its power.
Then Jesus speaks about fasting.
Again, He confronts people who deliberately alter their appearance so others will recognize their spirituality.
Different century.
Same heart.
They wanted suffering to become a costume.
They wanted sacrifice to become advertising.
They wanted people to look at them and think:
Wow. That person must really love God.
Jesus tells His followers, essentially, not to turn devotion into theater.
There is something almost breathtaking about His alternative.
Live before the Father.
Give before the Father.
Pray before the Father.
Fast before the Father.
Stop needing every act of obedience to produce witnesses.
Some of the holiest moments of your life may happen where nobody can photograph them.
Some of your greatest victories may receive no comments.
Some of your deepest worship may never be heard by another human being.
Some of your most costly obedience may never become a testimony you tell publicly.
And it still matters.
Because God saw it.
But there is another danger here.
We can misunderstand Jesus and become afraid of doing anything publicly for God.
That is not what this passage teaches.
Remember Matthew 5:16.
Jesus wants good works to become visible in ways that cause people to glorify the Father.
Christianity was never meant to become invisible.
The Gospel is supposed to be proclaimed.
Mercy is supposed to spread.
Truth is supposed to be spoken.
People are supposed to hear about Jesus.
Testimonies can encourage believers.
Public generosity can sometimes inspire generosity.
Sharing Scripture can put God's Word in front of someone who desperately needs it.
A Christian ministry can invite people to participate in its mission.
The question is not merely:
“Will people see this?”
The question is:
“Whose glory am I seeking when they do?”
There is an enormous difference between making Christ visible and making yourself impressive.
And only God perfectly knows where that line runs through your heart.
Which means Matthew 6 should produce humility rather than suspicion.
“Search me, O God.”
Not:
“Search them, O God.”
Search me.
Why did I post that?
Why did I say that?
Why did it bother me when nobody thanked me?
Why was I disappointed when my name was not mentioned?
Why did I need people to know how much I sacrificed?
Why did being overlooked hurt so badly?
Why did somebody else's recognition feel like my rejection?
Why do I want people to think I am spiritually mature?
Why do I sometimes want the appearance of holiness more than the painful process of actually becoming holy?
Those questions hurt.
But sometimes grace begins where pretending ends.
And this is where we must be careful not to turn the Sermon on the Mount into another ladder by which sinners try to climb toward God.
Because if Matthew 6 only leaves you thinking, I need to purify my motives enough so God will accept me, you have not yet reached the Gospel.
Who among us has perfectly pure motives?
Who has never wanted approval?
Who has never enjoyed recognition too much?
Who has never mixed worship with ego?
Who has never wanted to appear better than he really was?
If acceptance before God depended upon perfectly unmixed motives, every one of us would be exposed.
We need more than behavioral adjustment.
We need mercy.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
And that is where Jesus becomes infinitely more than a moral teacher telling hypocrites to behave better.
The One preaching this sermon would eventually walk toward a cross.
Not surrounded by admirers.
Surrounded by mockers.
Stripped.
Rejected.
Humiliated.
His public image destroyed.
No earthly applause.
No attempt to impress the crowd.
He obeyed the Father all the way to death.
Jesus did not merely teach a righteousness deeper than performance.
He ultimately became the hope of performers, hypocrites, approval-addicts, sinners, and people like us whose motives have never been as pure as we pretend.
At the cross, our masks become useless.
We cannot impress God there.
We cannot perform our way into forgiveness.
We cannot accumulate enough Christian activity to erase our sin.
We come empty-handed.
We repent.
We believe.
We receive grace.
Christ died for sinners and rose again, and the Gospel does not merely polish our religious image.
It gives us a new life.
That is why the answer to spiritual performance is not better spiritual performance.
It is Jesus.
It is learning that because of Christ, you do not have to manufacture a righteous identity before other people.
Your salvation is not secured by their applause.
Your worth is not measured by their reaction.
Your standing before God is not determined by whether people think you are impressive.
Come to Christ honestly.
No costume.
No stage.
No carefully edited spiritual image.
Just the truth.
“Jesus, there is pride in me.”
“Jesus, I wanted people to notice.”
“Jesus, sometimes I wanted the reputation of holiness more than holiness.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
That prayer may be more beautiful before heaven than a thousand impressive performances.
Because repentance kills the illusion.
Grace meets the sinner underneath the costume.
And Jesus begins rewriting what pride tried to author.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal was never something that made headlines.
Maybe your scandal has lived quietly inside your motives.
The craving to be admired.
The obsession with being recognized.
The secret jealousy when somebody else receives attention.
The Christian image you have worked hard to protect.
The terror that people might discover you are weaker than they think.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling you closer.
Not closer to the stage.
Closer to Himself.
Maybe the freedom you desperately need begins when you stop asking:
“Did they see me?”
and start asking:
“Did He?”
Because your Father sees what is done in secret.
And that can become enough.
So do something this week that only God knows about.
Encourage someone anonymously if appropriate.
Give without announcing the amount.
Pray for someone who may never discover you prayed.
Serve where there is no photograph.
Forgive without turning your forgiveness into a testimony about how gracious you are.
Open your Bible without posting it.
Sit with Jesus when nobody is watching.
And when your flesh whispers, But nobody knows…
answer it:
My Father knows.
That is enough.
And ironically, this truth also changes how we share the Gospel publicly.
Sharing something about Christ is not automatically spiritual performance.
If your purpose is genuinely to help someone see Jesus, sharing can become service.
And if these words exposed something uncomfortable, do not hide behind silence simply to preserve an image.
Be honest.
Your honesty may give somebody else permission to stop pretending too.

And if Gospel Warrior is helping you grow deeper in Scripture, you can follow and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well—not to build a personality cult, but so more people can encounter daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the message of Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus.
It does not.
And certainly not because God can be manipulated into blessing someone who financially supports a ministry.
He cannot.
Support Christian work because you have already received grace—not because you are trying to purchase it.
Your support helps us keep putting Scripture, Gospel-centered encouragement, discipleship materials, and Christian resources in front of people who may desperately need them.
But remember the warning that began this entire conversation.
Do not comment because everyone else is commenting.
Do not perform.
Love.
Do not advertise yourself.
Point to Jesus.
Do not chase the reward of being seen.
Live before the Father who already sees.
Because one day the likes disappear.
The applause stops.
The audience goes home.
The reputation fades.
The platform belongs to somebody else.
And eventually every carefully constructed version of ourselves falls away.
Then only truth remains.
Christ remains.
Grace remains.
And perhaps one of the greatest freedoms Jesus can give you in this life is the ability to do something beautiful for Him…
and be completely at peace when nobody knows.
When you no longer need the crowd to see you, you finally discover how deeply the Father always has.
